transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Lunaris Head of ML), David Ortiz (Lunaris Infra), Priya Rao (Prod)

Summary: quick review of last week's benchmark numbers, deeper look at tokens/sec per dollar across hosted vs dedicated, discussion on caching savings and batching tradeoffs. Agreed next steps to run additional KV-cache + batching benchmarks on Lunaris sample workload and update ROI spreadsheet.

[00:00] Samira: ok hey everyone thanks for joining, looks like we have most of the team, Maya, Priya, David, you there?
[00:07] Maya: yep here, thanks Samira.
[00:09] Priya: hi, yep.
[00:11] David: morning.
[00:13] Samira: great. quick agenda - review the numbers Ethan sent, talk caching / batching tradeoffs, then next steps. Ethan do you want to kick off with the benchmark recap?
[00:22] Ethan: sure, yeah. so last week we ran three primary configs against Lunaris's sample traces: baseline hosted model with default batching (auto), then an optimized batching config, and then the same with prefix/KV cache enabled. I put the CSV in the shared drive - link in the invite. quick headline: optimized batching bumped tokens/sec by ~2.6x and reduced per-token $ by about 38% for the chat endpoint on our test corpus. enabling prefix cache further reduced token generation work for the 40% of requests that are repeated prefixes, giving you roughly another 15-20% unit cost reduction in those flows.
[01:05] Maya: okay when you say 40% repeated prefixes that's across the sample trace? is that realistic for our prod traffic?
[01:12] Ethan: it's from the sample you provided - the FAQ/help endpoint and the few templated flows have very high prefix reuse. we saw about 42% of tokens saved on those paths specifically; overall system-level saving averaged 12-18% depending on distribution.
[01:25] David: can you remind me the exact numbers for p50 and p95 latency in the batching runs? latency is our big concern.
[01:32] Ethan: yeah. baseline p50 was 120 ms, p95 around 420 ms. with batching=64 p50 went to 180 ms, p95 to 520 ms - so some increase, but tokens/sec improved from ~650 to ~1700. with batching plus cache p50 was ~160 ms, p95 ~480 ms, because cache avoids generating many tokens at all. So tradeoffs: better throughput and lower cost but higher tail latency unless we tune target batch sizes per route.
[02:05] Priya: could we do adaptive batching? like smaller batches for customer-facing low-latency endpoints and larger batches for background inference?
[02:13] Ethan: absolutely, Redwood supports per-route batching policies and you can set target latency SLOs. we can configure one route to stay under 150 ms p95 with smaller batches and let others use aggressive batching. the runtime's smart routing can also send requests to a lower-cost pool if latency isn't critical.
[02:31] Maya: what's the cost delta between hosted and dedicated for our scale? rough numbers are fine.
[02:36] Samira: from the scenarios we sketched: for your current pilot throughput (approx 5M tokens/day), hosted is about $0.048/token - sorry, that was a placeholder - let me give per-token units: hosted (our curated open model) ~ $0.000012/token at baseline config; with optimized batching and caching we project effective cost down to ~ $0.000007/token. Dedicated reserved capacity with similar performance can bring unit cost further down but you pay a monthly commit; at your current 5M tokens/day, Dedicated ROI breaks even around month 3-4 depending on commit size and utilization.
[03:20] David: that per-token number seems lower than our expectations, are we including infra amortization?
[03:24] Ethan: yes it's model+serving amortized; the dedicated number assumes high utilization on the reserved pool. if your usage spikes only seasonally, the math shifts. Samira will add a few scenarios into the ROI sheet.
[03:36] Priya: also curious how quantization affects quality vs cost; we saw some small regressions last week with 4-bit.
[03:44] Ethan: right - quantization profile matters. 4-bit q4-like profiles gave 25-35% throughput improvements and similar token-level cost decreases but some small fidelity regressions on edge cases. For customer-facing prompts we recommend q8 or mixed-precision; for bulk rerank or embeddings, q4 is usually fine. we can run your eval set to measure regression rates and flag any quality thresholds.
[04:06] Maya: can you explain caching more - what's KV-cache vs prefix cache? I get them mixed up.
[04:12] Ethan: sure. prefix cache stores completed model outputs for an exact input prefix (like frequently repeated prompts). KV-cache here means storing key/value states for autoregressive decoding so when you see the same prefix you can reuse part of the decoder state rather than recomputing from scratch - in practice Redwood uses both: exact match prefix cache for 1:1- identical queries, and KV reuse to speed up similar sequences. both reduce compute but have different hit rates.
[04:39] Maya: hit rates on our sample looked high for prefix cache on FAQ flows but low for free-form analytics queries, correct?
[04:45] Ethan: correct. so we advised a hybrid strategy: enable prefix cache for the FAQ route and aggressive batching; keep analytics endpoints with smaller batches and optional cache TTLs.
[04:55] Samira: quick note on billing: our hosted billing shows both raw token counts and effective billed tokens after cache hits; we can show tokens saved vs billed tokens in the invoice.
[05:05] Priya: that's helpful. can invoices reflect cached token savings? we need that for finance.
[05:09] Samira: yes we can provide a detailed breakdown export.
[05:12] David: network & security question - if we go Dedicated, can we do VPC peering and keep logs in our KMS?
[05:19] Ethan: Dedicated supports private peering, VPC/VPN options and you can integrate customer-managed KMS/HSM for key wrapping. audit logs can be pushed to your logging endpoint, and we support SOC2 artifacts. there are some constraints on very strict air-gapped deployments - that's more Private deployment territory.
[05:37] Maya: are there differences in caching when you run Dedicated vs Hosted? e.g., cache locality benefits?
[05:43] Ethan: good question. with Dedicated, you control the pool and caching is local to that pool so hit rates are higher if most of your traffic uses that pool. hosted is multi-tenant but our runtime segments caches per-tenant; with very bursty usage Dedicated tends to give more consistent cache hit rates because the working set stays in the same pool.
[06:00] Priya: ok let's talk tokens/sec per dollar - do you have an explicit formula you use?
[06:06] Ethan: yes, roughly tokens_per_sec / (cost_per_second) but we usually compute tokens-per-dollar as tokens_per_sec * 3600 / cost_per_hour. practically we run end-to-end bench for a config, measure sustained tokens/sec and divide by cost of infra + model for that config. the sheet I shared has the apple-to-apple numbers.
[06:27] Maya: could you walk through one example from the CSV? like batching=64 + cache for the chat route?
[06:33] Ethan: sure: for that config on 4xA100-equivalent pool we saw sustained 1,700 tokens/sec; infra+model cost for that pool was $2.10/hour effective for the portion used by the route, so tokens per dollar = 1,700 * 3600 / 2.10 ≈ 2,914,286 tokens per $1. Compared to baseline 650 tokens/sec and cost $1.80/hour ≈ 1,300,000 tokens per $. So roughly 2.2x better tokens/$ for the optimized config.
[07:12] David: wow those numbers are good; are those all synthetic or from our trace?
[07:16] Ethan: a mix - we've replayed your trace through the runtime; the tokens/sec is from real-time replay with similar request mix. end-to-end latency was measured with synthetic concurrency that matches your observed concurrencies.
[07:28] Maya: i'm nervous about p95 tail with batching 64 on customer-facing things. is there a way to get the cost benefits while keeping p95 < 300 ms?
[07:37] Ethan: yes - a few options: dynamic batching (route-level target latency), priority queues (low-latency requests preempt batch assembly), or a two-tier pool where a small fraction of traffic goes to a low-latency pool and the rest to a high-throughput pool. cost wise the two-tier approach usually gets you 80-90% of the cost savings while keeping critical traffic latency tight.
[08:00] Priya: any quick numbers on two-tier? like what % to put in low-latency?
[08:04] Ethan: based on your traffic mix, if you put 15-20% of requests in low-latency pool you'll satisfy most interactive SLOs and still get ~70-75% of batching savings. we can simulate different splits.
[08:18] Samira: can i flag a small ask - for finance we need a conservative scenario, an expected, and an optimistic with caching fully effective. can you produce those three in the spreadsheet?
[08:28] Ethan: yes i can. i'll produce Conservative (no cache, batching minimal), Expected (batching optimized, partial cache), Optimistic (aggressive batching + high cache hit) with tokens/$ and monthly cost numbers.
[08:39] Maya: awesome. on the eval side, we need to see LM quality delta for quantization profiles across 200 eval prompts. that will determine if q4 is acceptable for some endpoints.
[08:47] Ethan: we'll run q8/q4/mixed on your eval set and output a simple delta table with thresholds.
[08:54] David: any PCI or PII concerns with caching? like if we cache user PII in prefix cache, how do we avoid storing sensitive info?
[09:01] Ethan: good point. we have TTLs and redaction hooks. Redwood's cache policies allow you to exclude routes or scrub tokens before they hit cache. for PII you can disable caching or apply deterministic redaction. also customer-managed KMS ensures ciphertext keys are controlled by you.
[09:20] Priya: nice. a few clarifying questions from finance: do you show token savings as negative billed tokens or as a credit?
[09:27] Samira: it's shown as billed tokens after cache; invoice line items show raw tokens, cache hits, and effective billed tokens plus dollar amount. we can also provide a reconciliation CSV.
[09:34] Maya: do you have any recommended default batching targets per endpoint type? like search vs chat vs analytics?
[09:40] Ethan: yes, general guidance: search/rerank can use large batch sizes (128-256), background analytics up to 512 if you have long sequences, chat endpoints usually 32-64, interactive customer-facing chat we recommend 8-32 depending on SLO. these are starting points; we'll tune per-route.
[09:57] David: on Dedicated sizing - how many GPUs in a pool would you recommend for our projected steady-state?
[10:03] Ethan: for 5M tokens/day with your current concurrency profile i'd recommend a small reserved pool of 4 x A100-equivalent instances with an autoscale headroom of 2. that typically covers steady-state plus bursts; we can refine after you share token histograms.
[10:16] Maya: what about cold-starts when autoscaling - do we lose cache warmness?
[10:20] Ethan: yes scaling up new workers will have cold caches; that's why we recommend reserved headroom and pre-warming strategies for scheduled spikes. Dedicated makes this easier because you control scale and can keep a minimal always-on footprint.
[10:33] Priya: ok i'm going to ask the hard question: what's the single biggest risk for us moving forward?
[10:37] Maya: (laugh) it's probably Prod.
[10:39] Ethan: i'd say two things: quality regression from aggressive quantization and variability in cache hit rates if your traffic distribution changes. both are manageable but need monitoring and eval gating.
[10:49] Samira: cool - let's wrap with next steps and owners. we captured most of them in the action items. any final questions?
[10:56] Maya: none from me, thanks.
[10:58] David: all good.
[11:00] Priya: thanks everyone.
[11:02] Samira: thanks - we'll send the updated ROI and schedule the dedicated deep dive. bye.

Post-call notes: shared drive links - benchmark CSV (redwood/benchmarks/lunaris-mar04.csv), ROI template (redwood/sales/roi-lunaris-0304.xlsx), eval harness request (redwood/evals/lunaris-eval-request.md).

Explicit recap (from call):
- Benchmarks show ~2.2x tokens/$ improvement with batching=64 + cache on replayed trace; p95 latency increases but can be mitigated with routing policies.
- Cache effective for templated FAQ endpoints (40% prefix reuse); system-wide savings 12-18% on sample.
- Dedicated can further reduce unit cost but requires commit; recommend 4 GPUs reserved with 2 headroom as starting point.
- Risks: quantization quality delta, variable cache hit rates, cold-start cache warmness.

End of transcript.
